top_choice_rationale: P004 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) rests on two separable, roughly three-decade-old programmes: electoral rules and constitutions shaping fiscal policy, and the political determinants of state capacity. Each comes from a long-standing partnership, so credit is traceable, and the work has been extended across public finance, macro and development. Its weaknesses are partly observational cross-country identification and partial overlap with the 2024 institutions prize. A citation built on the formal framework and later sharper designs, with no causal claims drawn from cross-country regressions, mitigates both, and I read the overlap as partial because the 2024 prize concerned colonial and long-run institutional origins. P002 is a close second: its building blocks are separable and mature, but eight credited names and an unsettled choice between honouring the theoretical originators and the estimation strand make any trio contestable. P003 is the best-identified, most checkable evidence, but magnitude and persistence are debated, the task-framework credit lies outside the ballot, and Katz is excluded. P001 has the cleanest credit line, but the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum lineage is uncredited and its welfare magnitudes depend on functional form. All four are preferable to no award.
recusal_note: Profile-based connections, disclosed and not adjudicated. My dynamic political-economy and public-finance research is adjacent to the P004 field. The profile documents no co-authorship or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley. Any IIES connection to Persson is unverified. I co-authored a paper with Friberg, who also supports P004. I am an IIES colleague and frequent co-author of Krusell and Boppart, who support P002, and none of them is a credited candidate. My own co-authors (Storesletten, Zilibotti, Rodríguez Mora, Krusell, Olovsson) are not credited on any ranked proposal. My 2018 presentation speech and the cited Scientific Background do not establish a preference on this slate.
